n: In 711 BC the Assyrian commander-in-chief, sent by King Sargon II, captured the Philistine city of Ashdod, which had rebelled with hopes of Egyptian help. Sargon’s own records describe this campaign.

f.g: An Assyrian title for the commander-in-chief, not a personal name (2 Kings 18:17).
Sargon II, king of Assyria about 722–705 BC; named only here in the Bible.
One of the five main Philistine cities.

n: The Lord told Isaiah to remove his sackcloth and sandals. Isaiah obeyed and went about stripped down and barefoot — likely in just a loincloth, like a captive.

f.g: Coarse garment, perhaps a prophet’s typical clothing.
Probably meaning stripped of his outer garment, as prisoners were.

n: The Lord explains: Isaiah’s three years of going like this were a living sign about what would happen to Egypt and Cush (Ethiopia).

f.g: Cush — Nubia, whose kings then ruled Egypt.

n: So Assyria would lead away Egyptian and Cushite captives, young and old, stripped and barefoot, to their deep shame. Assyrian carvings show such lines of prisoners.

f.g: Assyria invaded Egypt in the 670s–660s BC.

n: Those who had placed their hopes in Cush and boasted of Egypt would be dismayed and ashamed.

f.g: What they looked to for help.

n: People of the coastland — Philistia and Judah — will say, “If even Egypt, whom we trusted, is captured, how can we escape Assyria?” The lesson: trust God, not political powers.

f.g: This coastland — the Mediterranean coast of Palestine.
